new_statements.rule_in_words: Kabwa is described as a tone language with a privative H vs toneless contrast, not as a stress language. Noun stems carry a lexical H in one of four lexically determined positions (final H, penult H, double H, antepenult H; Table 8), H spreads rightward in some contexts, and utterance-final H is deleted (so final-H and double-H nouns are all-low in isolation). Verb stems have no lexical tone; grammatical (melodic) H falls on the first syllable of the macrostem (infinitive: òkù-[ɾúmà 'to bite') or on the whole macrostem, some forms have H on the TAM prefix, and some forms are toneless. No word-stress rule is stated for Kabwa. The only stress remark anywhere is the Orthography Statement p. 8, which says a root long vowel in derived verbs 'is sometimes shortened in normal pronunciation, perhaps due to the stress placed on a later syllable' — an unanalysed hint that phonetic prominence falls late in the word (presumably the penult), not a rule.
new_statements.exceptions: Aunio et al. note that 'regular penultimate stress' exists only for some Zanaki speakers, possibly under Swahili influence, and weight-determined tone placement for Ngoreme; neither is said of Kabwa. Orthography Statement §2.3.1 (p. 15): only one tonal minimal pair found (omusimu 'arrow' vs 'season'), lexical tone judged to have low functional load and is not. §2.3.3 (p. 16): Remote Past has H on the verb root vs all-low General Present ([twaagúɾa] vs [twaaguɾa]).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level tonal analysis based on the authors' field data (SIL Kabwa team); tones cited are phrase-medial forms because utterance-final H is deleted in Kabwa (isolation/citation forms neutralise final-H and double-H nouns). Nouns and infinitives/inflected verbs both covered.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Kabwa proper (ISO cwa, Guthrie/Maho JE405), Mara Region, Tanzania; the Orthography Statement (§1.3, p. 6) states Kabwa 'is perceived internally as having only one dialect' (Kiroba and Sweta, its closest relatives, belong to Suba-Simbiti [ssc], suba1254). Aunio et al. 2019 treat Kabwa as one of six Mara corpus languages; the Kabwa data come from the SIL Kabwa team (Walker, Robinson). The SIL OAI record dates the orthography statement 2012 (Walker, Meszaros, Robinson) but the document itself is the 'Approved Orthography Edition: December 2017' authored by Rebekah Overton and John B. Walker (Meszaros and Overton are evidently the same person).

sources.note: §2.3 'Tone and syllable structure' (draft pp. 7-12): the six Mara languages incl. Kabwa are analysed as H vs Ø tone languages; Kabwa has lexical noun tone (incl. a double-H pattern), utterance-final H deletion, H spread, and melodic H on the first syllable of the macrostem or the whole macrostem in verbs. No word-stress statement for Kabwa; 'regular penultimate stress' is reported only for some Zanaki speakers ('possibly under Swahili influence').
